references.text: Hyssop is used in cleansing rituals, especially for leprosy, just as it was used to apply blood to the doorframes during Passover.
Hyssop is used together with cedar wood and scarlet yarn in the cleansing ritual involving the red heifer.
Hyssop dipped in water is used to cleanse people and objects that have become unclean.
David asks to be cleansed with hyssop, referring to the purifying role hyssop had in Israelite ritual practice.
Earlier in the same chapter, instructions are given to apply the blood to the doorframes and the upper lintel.
Explains why the blood on the doorframes offers protection—the Lord will pass over and not allow the destroyer to enter.
The Letter to the Hebrews refers to the use of hyssop and blood in covenant ceremonies and cleansing rituals, pointing forward to Christ's blood.
By faith Moses celebrated Passover and applied the blood to the doorframes so that the destroyer would not touch the firstborn.
At the crucifixion, a sponge soaked in vinegar was placed on a hyssop stalk and lifted up to Jesus, creating a connection with the Passover lamb.
Ezekiel 45:19 shows how the protective and sanctifying function of Passover blood continues in the future temple worship.
Contrasting uses of blood: on doorposts for deliverance from judgment (Exod 12), and on body parts for consecration to service (Exod 29).
Isaiah 26:20 alludes directly to Passover protection by using the image of shutting oneself inside to avoid God's wrath.
Rahab's house in Joshua 2:19 serves as a typological parallel to the Passover house in Exodus, where only those inside the door are saved.
Parallel ritualization of the house with hyssop; Exodus uses the lamb for protection from judgment, while Leviticus uses a bird for cleansing from infection.
